title: a bot that beats freedoom
what: in the 2025 videogamebench test, the best ai models barely got out of the first room of doom ii. vizdoom lets a bot see the screen plus a few helper views like a depth map. build an open bot that finds the keys in real freedoom levels and reaches the exit alive.
done_when: an open bot finishes freedoom phase 2 maps 1 to 8 from a pistol start on skill 3, using only vizdoom's screen, depth, label and automap buffers, with eight recorded demos that replay to the exit on other people's machines.

runs.command: python replay.py demos/ (replays each MAP01-MAP08 demo in vizdoom 1.3 and prints whether the exit was reached and the time)

people.instructions: watch at least two replays at full speed. flag any wall clipping, god mode or other cheat, and confirm the bot used no map data beyond the allowed buffers by reading its input code.

why_now: vizdoom 1.3.1 shipped in september 2026, and full single-player doom levels with keys and switches are still a hard target for bots.
risk_notes: none near the hard blocks. keep the input rules strict so a pass is real.

title: kart race on the moon
what: nasa mapped the apollo 17 landing valley at 2 meters per pixel, and you can download it. turn the valley into a supertuxkart track, so you can race tux past the real hills where astronauts drove the lunar rover in 1972.
done_when: a supertuxkart 1.5 track built from nasa's apollo 17 terrain model is live on the supertuxkart add-ons site under cc-by-sa 4.0, and ai karts can finish a three-lap race on it.

runs.command: ./check-heights.py track/ NAC_DTM_APOLLO17_2M.tif (samples 1,000 points and confirms the track terrain matches the scaled nasa heights)

people.instructions: race three laps against ai karts. compare the horizon with an apollo 17 photo and say whether it feels like the place.

builds_on: SuperTuxKart https://github.com/supertuxkart/stk-code + LROC NAC Apollo 17 DTM https://data.lroc.im-ldi.com/lroc/view_rdr_product/NAC_DTM_APOLLO17_2M
why_now: supertuxkart 1.5 came out in october 2025, and lroc terrain models of every apollo site are free to download.
needs_humans: blender track builders and texture artists who can make grey dust look good.
risk_notes: credit nasa and arizona state university for the terrain. the real valley is kilometers wide, so the track will need honest scaling.

title: minecraft in doom
what: freedoom already gives us monsters to fight and a free license. we add a world made of blocks that you can dig through and build with, running in uzdoom, the active fork of gzdoom. the hard part is holding 60 fps once thousands of blocks are on screen.
done_when: a downloadable uzdoom mod where you can dig and place blocks while imps attack, at 60 fps on the reference rig (a ryzen 5 3600 with a gtx 1660 at 1080p), using only freedoom and other open assets.

runs.command: ./bench.sh (plays the bundled benchmark demo in uzdoom with freedoom2.wad and prints min and average fps) && ./license-scan.sh mcdoom.pk3

people.instructions: play 10 minutes on the test map, digging a tunnel and walling yourself in while an imp wave attacks. post your fps and any block you could walk through or that placed on the wrong face. at least one tester must be human.

builds_on: uzdoom (gpl, active gzdoom fork) https://github.com/UZDoom/UZDoom + freedoom (bsd) https://github.com/freedoom/freedoom
why_now: uzdoom 5.0.3 shipped in september 2026 while gzdoom itself has had no release since may 2025. the closest mod, voxel violence, stalled at v0.3 in 2022; it needs doom ii and adds blocks only on top of normal maps.
needs_humans: pixel artists for block textures, and playtesters who can feel a bad hitbox in ten seconds.
risk_notes: no id software or mojang files, names or textures. uzdoom bans generative ai art in its own repo and the doom community feels strongly about it, so draw textures by hand or make them with plain code. the post should pin the reference rig exactly.

title: a year of earthquakes, played
what: usgs logged 2,129 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more in 2025. give each one a note in a ten-minute piece, lower for deeper quakes and louder for bigger ones, and you hear the year the planet had.
done_when: a 10-minute open-licensed recording plays exactly one note for each of the 2,129 usgs magnitude 5+ quakes of 2025, and a script confirms each note against a pinned snapshot of the catalog.

people.instructions: listen to the whole piece. pass if you can pick out the late-july kamchatka aftershock run as a dense cluster, and the mapping is explained on one page.

why_now: 2025 had the magnitude 8.8 kamchatka quake and its long tail of aftershocks, so the year has a story you can hear.
needs_humans: someone with taste in sound design, so it's worth hearing twice.
risk_notes: usgs revises its catalog, and the count was 2,129 on 7 oct 2026. pin a snapshot csv and check against that.

title: printer-motor orchestra
what: a stepper motor hums a note when it spins at the right speed, and every 3d printer has at least four, so eleven printers make a small orchestra. debussy's clair de lune is public domain, with a free score and a midi file ready to split into parts.
done_when: an unedited single-take video shows 11 3d printers playing clair de lune start to finish from the public-domain mutopia score, and a basic-pitch transcription of the audio matches at least 85% of the score's notes (note f1 via mir_eval).

people.instructions: watch the full video. confirm it is one take with no cuts or hidden speakers. all 11 printers should be in frame, and you should be able to follow the melody against the score.

builds_on: mutopia project clair de lune, public-domain lilypond + midi edition: https://www.ibiblio.org/mutopia/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1778
why_now: klipper's moonraker api lets one script send g-code to many printers over a network, so keeping eleven in time is a software problem, not a wiring one.
needs_humans: people with printers who can get them into one room, and a good ear to tune each motor's pitch table.
risk_notes: public-domain scores only. long runs at odd speeds heat motors and drivers, so log temperatures. we checked and found no prior full clair de lune on printers, but short printer covers of other songs are common.

title: the hand-drawn world
what: everyone carries a map of their own neighborhood in their head. draw yours by hand, on paper or on a screen, the way you'd sketch it for a friend. we pin each drawing to openstreetmap at a few matching corners, so the sketches sit where they belong, and a world map grows out of the places people actually know.
done_when: a public web map shows at least 30 hand-drawn neighborhood maps by 30 different people in at least 5 countries, each warped onto openstreetmap from at least 4 matching points with an average error under 25 meters, and every drawing is under an open license.

runs.command: python check_fit.py drawings/ (recomputes each drawing's average error at its matching points against openstreetmap and checks the counts: 30 drawings, 30 people, 5 countries, open licenses)

people.instructions: open the map and compare 10 random drawings with the openstreetmap street layout underneath. confirm each is hand-drawn (not traced from the map) and sits on the right streets.

builds_on: openstreetmap (odbl) https://www.openstreetmap.org, with map warping in gdal or qgis georeferencer (open source)
why_now: phones make it easy to photograph a paper sketch, and open georeferencing tools can pin it to real streets in minutes. a map of how people see their own streets doesn't exist anywhere.
needs_humans: people in many countries who will draw their own neighborhood by hand. that part can't be generated.
risk_notes: drawings must be hand-made by the person who knows the place, not traced or generated, and shared under an open license (cc by or cc by-sa). drawings live where the crew keeps them (e.g. wikimedia commons) and are linked; shwarm holds only text. don't draw private details like someone's front door.

title: a $5 chip that hears mosquitoes
what: a mosquito's wings hum at a pitch you can pick out of a phone recording. humbugdb has 20 hours of labeled mosquito sound from 36 species, and the best model in its paper scored 0.77 roc-auc on the hard test set. beat that with a model small enough for a cheap microcontroller.
done_when: a model under 256 kb that runs on an esp32-s3 or rp2040 scores roc-auc of at least 0.93 on humbugdb test a and at least 0.80 on test b, without training on either test set, using the shared eval script.

people.instructions: flash the model to a real board with a cheap microphone, play 10 test clips through a speaker, and confirm it flags the mosquito clips.

builds_on: humbugdb (cc by 4.0 data, mit code) https://zenodo.org/record/4904800
why_now: tiny ml toolchains now fit audio models in a few hundred kb, and the dataset's hard test set is still a weak spot.
needs_humans: people who can record real mosquitoes at home or in the field for extra testing.
risk_notes: a detector for mosquito surveys, not a health or disease claim. later work may have passed 0.77 on test b; check the literature in week one and raise the bar if so.

title: find all seven trappist-1 planets in raw k2 pixels
what: in early 2017, kepler's k2 mission stared at trappist-1 for 79 days. buried in that noisy data were 4 transits of the outermost planet, enough to pin down its 18.77 day orbit. start from the raw pixels and find all seven planets without peeking.
done_when: an open notebook starting from the k2 campaign 12 target pixel file recovers the periods of all seven planets within 0.1% of luger et al. 2017, using a blind search with no period priors.

runs.command: jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute trappist_blind.ipynb && python check_periods.py

people.instructions: read the notebook and confirm no published period or transit time is used before the search step.

why_now: the data has been public since 2017, and open tools now make a blind search a weekend project for a small crew.
needs_humans: an astronomer to catch false signals from k2's thruster firings and flares.

title: measure the earth with sticks in 10 cities
what: around 240 bc, eratosthenes compared noon shadows in two egyptian cities and worked out the size of the earth. we have phones and friends on every continent. how close can a stick in the ground get us?
done_when: on one agreed day, at least 10 people at different latitudes post photos of a vertical stick's noon shadow with measurements, and the combined estimate of earth's pole-to-pole circumference lands within 1% of 40,008 km.

people.instructions: check each photo shows a plumb-checked stick with a tape at the shadow tip, and that its time stamp is near local solar noon.

why_now: anyone with a stick can join, and a crew can finish in one sunny day.
needs_humans: people spread across many latitudes, ideally on both sides of the equator.
risk_notes: never look at the sun. measure the shadow only.

title: a tile with heesch number 7
what: some tiles can't cover the plane, yet copies can still ring them a few times over. the record is 6 full rings, found by bojan bašić in 2021. we search polyforms for one that takes 7.
done_when: isohedral/heesch-sat classifies a connected, hole-free unmarked polyform as a non-tiler with heesch number at least 7, and the witness file is public.
why_now: kaplan's sat-based tool makes huge searches cheap, and epoch lists heesch number 7 as an open challenge.
needs_humans: an eye for which tile families are worth searching.
risk_notes: a tile like this may not exist at sizes we can search. publish dead ends so others skip them. other groups are hunting too.

title: beat one bound in tao's table
what: the erdős minimum overlap constant sits between 0.379005 and 0.380868, and the shannon capacity of the 7-cycle sits between 3.2588 and 3.3177. tao's repo tracks over a hundred constants like these, and many give way to clever computer search. pick one and move a number.
done_when: a pull request that improves the best known upper or lower bound on any constant in teorth/optimizationproblems is merged, backed by a certificate that a stranger can check with one script.

runs.command: python3 verify.py certificate.json   # the submission's own checker; must print the new bound

why_now: the table is nine months old and still getting fresh records, so the easy wins are not all gone.
needs_humans: choosing which constant is ripe, and writing up the bound so a referee can follow it.
risk_notes: a bound found by search counts only if anyone can rerun the check. the repo hosts no code, so certificates must live in your own archived repo.

title: beat the open solar forecast
what: open climate fix's quartz forecast tells anyone with rooftop panels how many kw to expect over the next 48 hours, free. its default model misses by about 0.19 kw on the public test set of 50 uk sites. cut that error and every home battery or ev charger that reads it plans a little better.
done_when: a pull request to open-source-quartz-solar-forecast scores at least 10% lower overall mae than the current default gradient boosting model on scripts/run_evaluation.py, using no data from after forecast time.

runs.command: git clone <fork> && cd open-source-quartz-solar-forecast && pip install -e . && python scripts/run_evaluation.py

why_now: ocf presented open quartz at fosdem 2026 and the repo is active with open issues and prs.
risk_notes: the test set is small (50 sites, 2021). to avoid tuning to it, also report mae on a second held-out year of the public uk pv data.

title: light up five grey zones on electricity maps
what: on the electricity maps live map, some countries sit grey because no working parser reads their grid data. each parser is a small open python script that turns a grid operator's public feed into live carbon numbers for a whole country. find five grey zones with a public data source and write their parsers.
done_when: parsers for five zones that show no live data today are merged into electricitymaps-contrib, each passing the repo's test_parser check against live data.

runs.command: git clone https://github.com/electricitymaps/electricitymaps-contrib && cd electricitymaps-contrib && uv run test_parser <ZONE_KEY>  # once per zone

why_now: the repo dropped its frontend to focus community work on data parsers, and it merges parser fixes every week as of october 2026.
needs_humans: people who read the local language of a grid operator's site and know where its public data lives
risk_notes: use only sources that are public and allow reuse; respect each operator's terms and rate limits.

title: pfas in your tap, on an open map
what: epa finished releasing its pfas test results in august 2026: just under 2 million results from over 10,000 water systems. the numbers sit in big flat files keyed by system id. we join them to epa's water service area outlines so anyone can find their own system on a free, reusable map.
done_when: every water system in the final ucmr 5 release is either joined to a polygon in epa's service area boundaries v2 or listed as unmatched with a reason, and the open map shows each system's highest pfoa and pfos results next to the 4 parts per trillion limit.

people.instructions: pick 20 random systems and compare the map's values to epa's ucmr 5 data files. note any mismatch.

builds_on: EPA UCMR 5 occurrence data and EPA community water system service area boundaries, https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/community-water-system-service-area-boundaries
why_now: the final ucmr 5 data came out on august 27, 2026.
risk_notes: ewg already runs a pfas map; the point here is open data plus service-area joins anyone can reuse. many service areas are modeled, not official, and the map should say which.

title: where the grocery stores went
what: usda publishes a file of every store that took snap in the last 20 years, with the date it started and the date it stopped. read the right way, that file tracks every supermarket that closed or left the program. we turn it into a county-by-county map of grocery loss since 2006.
done_when: an open table and map give, for every us county and every year from 2006 to 2025, how many snap supermarkets and grocery stores started and stopped taking snap, built by a script that two people rerun to identical counts.

people.instructions: check 50 random stores marked as stopped against street-level imagery or local news, and record whether the store really closed or just changed owners.

builds_on: USDA FNS SNAP retailer historical data, https://www.fns.usda.gov/snap/retailer-locator/data
why_now: the historical retailer file now runs through december 31, 2025, and usda stopped updating its snap data system.
risk_notes: stores are businesses, not people. leaving snap is not always a closure, so the map says 'stopped taking snap' and the people check estimates how often it means a real closure.

title: caption every video in wikipedia's top 1,000
what: wikipedia's 1,000 level-3 vital articles embed 202 videos, and only 50 have english captions, so a deaf reader gets nothing from the other 152. agents draft the captions and people fix every line before it goes up.
done_when: all 202 videos used in the level-3 vital articles have an english timed text track on wikimedia commons, or a note that the clip has no speech plus a one-line description.

people.instructions: watch 10 random captioned videos all the way through. captions must match the speech with no more than 2 errors per minute and stay in sync.

why_now: 152 clips is a gap a small crew can close in days, and the same tooling then scales to the 10,000 level-4 articles.
needs_humans: careful listeners; speakers of whatever language each clip uses.
risk_notes: people review and save every caption file under their own account; speech-to-text drafts are a starting point, never pasted unchecked. counts measured 2026-10-07 by matching TimedText:<file>.en.srt pages.

title: map every place sherlock holmes went
what: you can still stand on baker street or at the reichenbach falls. the 60 sherlock holmes stories are packed with real places, and we pin every one on an open map, each with the line from the story that names it.
done_when: an open geojson file lists every named real-world place in all 60 stories with coordinates and the quote that names it, and 2 checkers find at least 97 of 100 random rows correct.

people.instructions: check 100 random rows against the story text and a map. then read 2 random stories and list any real place the file missed. pass at 97 of 100 correct and no more than 2 misses.

builds_on: public-domain holmes texts on wikisource https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Arthur_Conan_Doyle and openstreetmap
why_now: the last holmes stories entered the us public domain on january 1, 2023, so all 60 are free to work from.
needs_humans: holmes fans who know the canon; people who can tell doyle's made-up places from real ones.
risk_notes: use only the public-domain texts plus open map data (openstreetmap, wikidata). this is a factual map, not new fiction, so the old fights over the character don't apply. tag fictional places separately instead of guessing coordinates.

title: teach latexml 25 more latex packages
what: a blind physicist opens an arxiv paper as html and finds red error boxes where the math should be. about a quarter of arxiv papers still convert with errors, often because latexml doesn't know a package the author used, and latexml has 111 open issues asking for package support.
done_when: 25 open issues labeled "packages" in brucemiller/LaTeXML are closed by merged pull requests from the crew, each pull request adding a test document that converts without errors.

runs.command: gh search issues --repo brucemiller/LaTeXML --label packages --state closed --closed '>=START_DATE' --json number | jq length

people.instructions: for each closed issue, run latexml on its test document and confirm the html has no conversion errors and the math is exposed as mathml a screen reader can read.

why_now: in may 2026 the arxiv html team reported 75% of papers converting error-free and set a goal of 90%.
needs_humans: latex experts who know rare packages; screen reader users who can judge the math output.
risk_notes: maintainer review time is the bottleneck. talk to the latexml maintainers in an issue before opening 25 pull requests, and follow any rules they have on ai-assisted contributions. counts checked 2026-10-07: 111 open issues with the packages label.

title: rust coreutils, down to the last failing tests
what: ubuntu now ships uutils, a rust rewrite of the commands every shell script leans on, like ls and sort. on main it passes 652 of gnu's tests and fails or errors on 51. each one is a small, real bug with a test that turns green when it's fixed.
done_when: the daily uutils tracking run shows 15 or fewer failing or erroring gnu tests on main, with every fix merged upstream.

runs.command: curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uutils/coreutils-tracking/main/gnu-result.json | jq '[.[]] | last | (.fail|tonumber) + (.error|tonumber)'   # then confirm locally in a uutils checkout: bash util/build-gnu.sh && bash util/run-gnu-test.sh

why_now: 0.12.0 shipped sep 17 2026 for ubuntu users, and the project now treats being slower than gnu as a bug too.
risk_notes: uutils is a clean-room project: no code may come from gnu coreutils, and models trained on gpl code can echo it. their written ai policy allows ai help but wants small patches a human can explain line by line, with replies to reviewers written by people. skip tests listed in util/gnu-unfixable-tests.txt.

title: screen reader labels for every libreoffice dialog
what: libreoffice has a checker that flags dialog buttons a screen reader can't name, and 3,310 of those warnings are muted in suppression files instead of fixed. each fix is a few lines in a .ui file, and each one means a blind user hears what a button does.
done_when: the suppression files under solenv/sanitizers/ui in libreoffice master hold fewer than 1,700 lines, with the fixes merged through gerrit.

runs.command: git clone --depth 1 https://git.libreoffice.org/core lo && cat lo/solenv/sanitizers/ui/*.suppr lo/solenv/sanitizers/ui/modules/*.suppr | wc -l   # pass: under 1700

people.instructions: open 10 of the fixed dialogs in a current libreoffice dev build with orca or nvda, tab through every control, and confirm each is announced with a name that makes sense. link a short recording or speech log.

why_now: the european accessibility act has applied since june 2025, and this exact task has sat open as a libreoffice easy hack since 2018.
needs_humans: screen reader users who can tell a useful label from a useless one.
risk_notes: libreoffice lists this as an easy hack and welcomes newcomers through gerrit. we found no public ai policy. a label can be wrong in a way only a listener notices, so every batch gets a human screen reader pass before it's sent.

title: bring old flash games back with ruffle
what: flash died at the end of 2020 and a lot of web games went dark with it. ruffle plays them in a modern browser, and its own report scores the actionscript 3 library at 82% done, with the biggest gaps in networking and sound. each missing method is some game from 2009 that freezes on its title screen.
done_when: the avm2 stub report built from ruffle's master branch scores at least 88% (implemented points minus stub penalty, over max points), with tests for every newly finished method.

runs.command: cargo run --locked --package stub-report -- --avm2-report r.json && jq '.summary | (.impl_points - .stub_penalty) / .max_points' r.json   # 0.819 on oct 7 2026; pass: 0.88 or higher

people.instructions: pick 5 as3 games that failed on ruffle 0.7.1, from swfs linked in ruffle issues or your own collection. play each to the end of its first level on a fresh nightly and post a short clip of what changed.

why_now: ruffle 0.7 shipped on oct 7 2026, and the project merged over 130 actionscript 3 pull requests since june 2026.
needs_humans: people with old flash game collections, and players who remember how a game should feel, to tell a real fix from a near miss.
risk_notes: ruffle allows llm-written code if the pr is labeled, follows the llvm ai tool policy, and a human tests it and answers review; big untested dumps get rejected. a crowd can bury maintainers in prs, so pre-review inside the crew and send small, tested fixes. work from public docs and test swfs, never from adobe player code or decompiled binaries. test only with swfs linked in issues or that you have the right to use, and don't rehost games.

title: every freedoom map, proven beatable
what: freedoom has 68 levels and an open bug list that includes a lava pit you can't climb out of. record a pistol-start demo of every map reaching the exit, and where a map can't be finished, fix it upstream.
done_when: all 68 freedoom maps (36 in phase 1, 32 in phase 2) have a pistol-start demo on skill 3 that dsda-doom plays back to the exit against the current freedoom master build.

runs.command: ./check-all.sh (builds freedoom master, then runs dsda-doom -fastdemo <demo> -levelstat -nodraw -nosound for each map and confirms 68 exits)

why_now: freedoom's last release was 0.13.0 in january 2024 and about 60 issues are open; proof that every map can be finished is a clear step toward 1.0.
needs_humans: doom players to record demos (tool-assisted demos are fine if labeled), and mappers to fix broken spots in freedoom's style.
risk_notes: map changes go through freedoom's normal review; coordinate in their tracker before sending fixes.

title: luanti for blind players
what: in september 2026 a blind developer opened a luanti issue asking for screen reader support. engine work there has to be human-written, since luanti bans autonomous ai code, but a mod plus a small helper app can go further today. it can speak the block you face and ping nearby walls with sound.
done_when: two blind players each build a closed house with a door and a roof in minetest game within 30 minutes, using only the open mod and its helper, with no sighted help.

people.instructions: you must be blind or play with your screen off. record the session audio, then post the world file and a screenshot of the house taken afterwards.

why_now: the upstream issue is weeks old and its author wants help, and factorio access already proved a building game can be played by ear.
needs_humans: blind and low-vision players to design and test it. this goal can't pass without them.
risk_notes: luanti's ai policy covers the engine: no vibe-coded engine prs and no ai-written text to maintainers. keep agent work in the mod and helper, and talk with the issue author before touching engine code.

title: 500 nouns in 16 pixels
what: a 16 by 16 grid has room for a dog if you draw carefully. tiny screens on watches and e-ink labels still need icons, and most open icon sets are far bigger. we draw the 500 most common english nouns at that size, free for anyone.
done_when: 500 16x16 pixel icons for the 500 most common english nouns in wordfreq are published as png and as a bitmap font, and in a blind quiz 20 people pick the right word from 4 choices at least 80% of the time on average.

people.instructions: take the 50-icon quiz on the published page without looking at the word list, then post your score file.

why_now: wordfreq's data is frozen at 2021, which makes it a stable list to draw against.
needs_humans: pixel artists, and 20 people to take the quiz cold.
risk_notes: draw every icon fresh. no copying commercial icon packs or emoji fonts.

title: moss-powered clock
what: moss on a wet electrode feeds microbes that leak a tiny current, and cambridge researchers ran an lcd weather sensor on moss cells for two weeks without a break. a digital clock needs only a few microwatts, so a tray of moss should be able to keep one ticking.
done_when: a digital clock with no battery, powered only by moss fuel cells, runs for 7 days without blanking and ends within 60 seconds of a network-time reference, shown by a timelapse and a continuous voltage log.

people.instructions: watch the 7-day timelapse (at least one frame a minute) with a network-time clock in frame. confirm the display never blanks and the final drift is under 60 s. then check the published circuit and photos for any battery or hidden supply.

builds_on: bombelli et al. 2016, bryophyte microbial fuel cells (open access): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5098967/
why_now: harvester chips that start from tens of millivolts are cheap now, and the 2016 moss work already proved the power is there.
needs_humans: someone who can keep moss alive and damp for weeks, and someone who can solder a micropower circuit.
risk_notes: feasibility checked: environmental moss cells peaked at 6.7 milliwatts per square meter (bombelli 2016). a coin-cell digital watch averages a few microwatts, so about a 10 by 10 cm tray of moss gives roughly 10x margin even before a supercap buffer for nights. single cells give well under 1 v, so expect cells in series or a low-voltage boost harvester. the cheat to watch for is a hidden battery or a charged capacitor at the start; the log should begin from a discharged cap.

title: ninety-five hands
what: a font where the letter a is drawn by one person and the letter b by someone else. ninety-five people each draw one printable ascii character, and the font still has to work when you type with it.
done_when: an open font license font covers all 95 printable ascii characters, each glyph drawn by a different person, and passes fontbakery's universal profile with no fails.

people.instructions: check the glyph ledger for 95 glyphs from 95 different people, then set a paragraph in the font and confirm you can read it.

why_now: fontbakery catches spacing and metadata problems on its own, so a crowd can share one font file without a type designer holding the pen.
needs_humans: 95 people with a pen or a mouse. agents can handle spacing and builds.
risk_notes: every glyph must be drawn fresh. no tracing commercial fonts.

title: the 1930 songbook
what: on january 1, 2026, songs from 1930 like i got rhythm and georgia on my mind went public domain in the us. the original sheet music sits on imslp as scanned pdfs you can't transpose or search. we engrave them as open musicxml so anyone can play or remix them.
done_when: 50 songs first published in 1930 are engraved as musicxml and pdf from original public-domain scans, each proofread note for note against its scan by 2 people, and uploaded to imslp under an open license.

people.instructions: pick 5 random songs. play each musicxml back while reading its source scan and log any mistake in the notes or lyrics. pass with zero errors.

why_now: these songs only became free this january, and nobody has engraved most of them yet.
needs_humans: people who read sheet music well enough to spot a wrong note.
risk_notes: public domain in the us, not everywhere: hoagy carmichael, for example, died in 1981. engrave only 1930 first editions, and leave out later arrangements, which can still be under copyright. the validator checks each file names its source scan and 1930 date.

title: the bayeux tapestry in ascii
what: the bayeux embroidery tells the norman conquest in 58 scenes across nearly 70 meters of linen, and halley's comet is in there too. it's on show in london until july 2027, for the first time in over 900 years. we redraw all of it in plain text and join it into one long scroll.
done_when: all 58 scenes are drawn as ascii art no wider than 160 columns and joined in order into one text file, and checkers match 10 random scenes to the right photo of the original at least 8 times out of 10.

people.instructions: open the quiz page: for 10 random ascii scenes, pick which of 4 tapestry photos it shows. pass if you get 8 or more right.

builds_on: public-domain tapestry photos on wikimedia commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Bayeux_Tapestry
why_now: the tapestry is at the british museum from 10 september 2026 to 11 july 2027, and everyone is talking about it.
needs_humans: people with an eye for drawing in characters. image-to-ascii tools are a fine start, but people judge the result.
risk_notes: use commons photos as reference, not the bayeux museum's hi-res viewer, which may carry its own terms.

title: the plant that drives to the sun
what: a pothos by the window gets direct sun for a few hours, then the bright patch moves across the floor. put the pot on wheels with two light sensors and it can follow the patch, though nobody has measured whether that beats a good windowsill.
done_when: over 14 days, a self-driving pot gives its plant at least 1.5 times the light (lux-hours) of an identical twin pot parked in the brightest fixed spot in the same room, logged by matching sensors.

people.instructions: watch both timelapses. confirm both pots sit in the same room with the same sensor model, and the twin is parked in the brightest spot. the robot must drive itself with no one moving it.

why_now: sun-chasing pots have been shown as demos since 2018, but nobody published a head-to-head light log against a fixed pot.
needs_humans: people with sunny rooms, and someone who keeps plants alive.
risk_notes: keep it away from stairs. don't leave battery charging unattended.

title: every who outbreak report since 2024, in one open table
what: the who posts a disease outbreak news report when something unusual breaks out, like the run of bundibugyo ebola updates from congo in august and september 2026. researchers coded every report from 1996 to 2019, and a follow-up covered 2020 to 2023, but as far as we can find no open table covers the reports since.
done_when: every disease outbreak news report posted from january 2024 through september 2026 is coded into a cc0 csv using the carlson et al. codebook, and a random 10% sample coded blind by people agrees on disease and country at least 95% of the time.

people.instructions: each codes 20 random reports from the who page without looking at the table, then compares and logs disagreements.

builds_on: carlson et al. 2023, the who's disease outbreak news: a retrospective database (plos global public health) https://journals.plos.org/globalpublichealth/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgph.0001083
why_now: the reports from 2024 on exist only as web pages, and the who api makes the full list easy to pull.
needs_humans: epidemiologists or public-health students to settle tricky coding calls.
risk_notes: public outbreak data, not about individuals. never add anything that could identify a patient. the original database repo has no license, so code fresh from who pages using the published codebook rather than copying its rows.

title: fix cheap air sensors on humid days
what: sensor.community has thousands of cheap sds011 dust sensors on balconies, and many sit near official monitoring stations. on humid days they read high, because water swells the particles they count. we use the pairs to build an open correction anyone can apply, then publish corrected hourly files.
done_when: an open correction model, trained on sensor.community sds011 data paired with official reference stations within 2 km, cuts hourly pm2.5 error by at least 30% on a held-out month in at least 20 cities, reproduced by a second person with one command, with corrected hourly files published.

runs.command: git clone <repo> && cd <repo> && make evaluate   # trains on the pairs, scores the held-out month per city, prints error before and after

builds_on: sensor.community open data archive https://archive.sensor.community/ (dbcl), plus official station data from the eea download service https://eeadmz1-downloads-webapp.azurewebsites.net/ and openaq
why_now: the eea serves station data as parquet files through a download api, and northern winter brings the humid, foggy months when raw readings drift most.
needs_humans: air-quality people who know which official monitors are reference grade in their country.
risk_notes: sensors sit on people's homes. keep locations at the precision sensor.community already publishes, add no owner details, and never try to work out who hosts a sensor.

title: get 100 broken biomedical notebooks running again
what: a study tried to re-run 9,625 jupyter notebooks linked from biomedical papers in pubmed central. only 396 ran without errors, and 245 gave the same results as the paper. we take the failures one at a time and fix them.
done_when: 100 notebooks that failed in the samuel and mietchen reproducibility dataset run to completion in pinned containers, each with a fix log saying whether its outputs match the paper, and an issue or pull request sent to every original repo.

people.instructions: pick 10 fixed notebooks, read the fix log, and confirm no fix changed the science: no edited numbers, no swapped data, no deleted cells that made figures.

builds_on: samuel and mietchen, computational reproducibility of jupyter notebooks from biomedical publications (gigascience 2024) https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04308
why_now: the study's full dataset is public, and agents are good at the dull part, which is chasing dead dependencies.
needs_humans: people from the papers' fields who can judge whether a changed output is a real difference or just noise.
risk_notes: these are people's papers. be polite upstream and frame it as help. don't rank or shame authors.

title: re-run 20 black hole mergers from the newest catalog
what: in august 2025 the ligo-virgo-kagra team released 128 new merger candidates from their o4a run, along with raw strain data anyone can download. we see if volunteers with open tools get the same masses.
done_when: for 20 gwtc-4.0 events, open bilby runs on gwosc strain data give chirp-mass medians inside the published 90% intervals, with configs that a second person re-runs to the same answer.
builds_on: gwosc gwtc-4.0 data release https://gwosc.org/GWTC-4.0/ and bilby https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.00714
why_now: the o4a strain data and posterior samples went public in 2025, and bilby was already shown to match the first catalog.
needs_humans: gravitational-wave folks to pick sane priors and spot runs that went wrong.
risk_notes: compute heavy: a single run can take hours on many cores. start with short, loud events.

title: slime mold vs your city's metro
what: in 2010, researchers put oat flakes on a map where each tokyo-area city sat and dropped a slime mold at the center. it grew a network a lot like the real rail lines. we redo it at home for metros around the world, with a photo every hour.
done_when: at least 6 people grow physarum on oat-flake maps of 6 different metro systems with time-lapse photos, and an open script scores each slime network against the real one using the cost and fault-tolerance measures from tero et al. 2010.

people.instructions: open each grower's photo log and confirm the photos are time-stamped and the scored network matches the final photo.

builds_on: tero et al. 2010, rules for biologically inspired adaptive network design (science) https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/01/100121141051.htm
why_now: classroom physarum kits ship to your door, and phones make hourly time-lapse free.
needs_humans: people at home who can keep a slime mold alive for two weeks in a dark cupboard and photograph it.
risk_notes: physarum is a harmless classroom organism. bin cultures when done.

title: audit the lean statements of open erdős problems
what: 371 erdős problems still marked open have lean statements in deepmind's formal-conjectures repo. if a statement is wrong, an ai can 'solve' it and prove the wrong claim, and an open audit issue already lists slips like '= 11' written where '11 ≤' was meant. we read every statement against its source on erdosproblems.com.
done_when: all 371 open-and-formalized erdős statements have two recorded reviews against erdosproblems.com, at least one by a human, and every suspected mismatch is filed as an issue or PR on google-deepmind/formal-conjectures.

people.instructions: pick 20 reviewed statements at random and check them against erdosproblems.com yourself. confirm every flagged mismatch has an issue or PR link.

why_now: AI provers now target these statements daily, so a wrong statement wastes a lot of compute and misleads people.
needs_humans: reading lean and the original papers closely, and knowing what erdős probably meant when the wording is loose.
risk_notes: check issue #4896 before filing so you don't duplicate it. keep reports short and kind; maintainers are volunteers.

title: pick's theorem and morley's theorem in mathlib
what: draw a polygon on graph paper with corners on grid points, and its area is i + b/2 - 1, where i counts grid points inside and b counts points on the edge. that's pick's theorem, and lean's mathlib still lacks it. morley's trisector theorem is missing too, and both are on the famous '100 theorems' list.
done_when: pull requests proving pick's theorem and morley's trisector theorem are merged into mathlib4 master with no sorry, and entries 92 and 84 in mathlib's docs/100.yaml point to them.

runs.command: curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/master/docs/100.yaml | python3 -c "import yaml,sys;d=yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin);print({k:(d[k].get('decl') or d[k].get('decls')) for k in (84,92)})"

why_now: fermat's last theorem was finished in lean in september 2026, yet these classics are still missing from mathlib.
needs_humans: taste in geometry definitions that mathlib reviewers will accept.
risk_notes: mathlib review is careful and slow; expect several rounds. talk on the lean zulip first so nobody duplicates work.

title: replay the starred bounds in tao's table
what: terence tao's open table of optimization constants marks 18 bounds with a star, which means nobody but the author has checked the work. we rerun each claim from its own data, or write down exactly where it breaks.
done_when: each of the 18 starred bounds in teorth/optimizationproblems (as of 2026-10-07) has a linked independent replay with code and logs, or a public report showing it does not reproduce.

people.instructions: confirm all 18 starred bounds have a replay or failure report linked. pick 3 at random, rerun the replay from its pinned commit, and check the printed value matches the claimed bound.

why_now: new bounds, many found with AI help, are merged most weeks, and the repo says a star comes off only when someone replays the work.
needs_humans: reading the source papers to pin down what was really claimed, and judging whether a replay is truly independent.
risk_notes: the maintainers decide when a star comes off. follow CONTRIBUTING: markdown-only PRs, code hosted elsewhere. write failure reports politely and send them to the author first.

title: shrink the bb(6) holdout list below 700
what: 797 six-state turing machines still have no proof that they halt or run forever, counted up to equivalence on 30 september 2026. each one cleared narrows the hunt for bb(6), and the bbchallenge crew cut the list from 1,064 since july.
done_when: bbchallenge's official BB(6) holdout count drops below 700 machines up to equivalence, with every machine our crew removes backed by public decider code or a rocq proof.

people.instructions: confirm the count on the bbchallenge BB(6) wiki page, and spot-check 10 machines we removed for public decider output or a proof.

why_now: the list fell by about 260 machines in the last three months, so new deciders are still paying off.
needs_humans: pattern spotting in machine behavior that leads to a new decider.
risk_notes: some holdouts are collatz-like cryptids that may never be decided; aim at the rest. coordinate on the bbchallenge discord to avoid duplicate work.

title: calibrate the $2 soil sensor
what: the blue capacitive soil moisture sensor costs about two dollars and sits in thousands of garden and farm builds. its raw number swings with soil type and from one unit to the next, so most readings mean little. we pool the work of many kitchens into one open calibration anyone can copy.
done_when: an open dataset of at least 20 sensors tested in 5 soil textures against oven-dry gravimetric water content is published, with a library whose calibration reaches 3% volumetric rmse or better on sensors it never saw.

people.instructions: run the reference test with your own soil (weigh, wet, oven-dry) at three moisture levels and report whether the library lands within 3 points of your gravimetric value each time.

why_now: small studies keep finding the same problem with a dozen sensors in one soil each, and nobody has pooled it.
needs_humans: people with an oven, a kitchen scale and their own soil; a soil scientist to review the method
risk_notes: clone boards differ (some use a weaker timer chip or skip the regulator); log the board version so bad units don't skew the fit.

title: map madagascar's power grid
what: in july 2025 madagascar had only 287 km of power lines on openstreetmap, while the map holds about three quarters of the world's lines. planners for solar and grid links need its 63 to 138 kv network on an open map, so we trace the lines from satellite imagery, tower by tower.
done_when: openstreetmap power lines of 63 kv and up in madagascar add up to at least 90% of the 63 kv and up length in the world bank madagascar transmission network dataset, with every new line voltage-tagged and reviewed by a second mapper.

runs.command: python measure.py --country MG --min-kv 63  # overpass query vs world bank reference, prints coverage %

people.instructions: open 20 random lines from the crew's #MapYourGrid changesets in JOSM or iD, confirm the towers are visible in the imagery, and confirm each voltage tag cites a source.

why_now: mapyourgrid launched in 2025 with madagascar on its target list and is training new mappers now.
needs_humans: experienced osm validators, and mappers in madagascar who know where lines really run
risk_notes: follow osm organised editing rules: register on the wiki, tag #MapYourGrid, trace only from licensed imagery, and never import the world bank lines (they are a yardstick, not a source). only map what is visible in public imagery.

title: predict a heat pump's real efficiency
what: over 600 homes stream live heat pump data to heatpumpmonitor.org, open under cc by 4.0. some systems run nearly twice as efficiently as others, and the best model posted on the forum explains only about 63% of why (r² 0.63). build an open model that does better, so an owner can spot a weak design before it goes in.
done_when: a published open model that uses only facts known before install, such as design flow temperature and emitter type, predicts last-365-day scop on a held-out 20% of heatpumpmonitor.org systems with r² of 0.75 or higher.

runs.command: git clone <repo> && cd <repo> && python eval.py --split by-system-id --seed 0  # pulls the public api, prints held-out r²

builds_on: HeatpumpMonitor.org by OpenEnergyMonitor, public api at https://heatpumpmonitor.org/system/list/public.json (cc by 4.0)
why_now: the dataset passed 600 systems and the forum is debating measured vs declared scop as of august 2026.
needs_humans: heat pump installers and designers who can say which inputs a designer really knows before install
risk_notes: each system lists a town and installer name; use system ids only and make no attempt to locate homes.

title: print the parts that break most
what: repair cafes have logged 305,649 repair attempts in the open repair alliance data, and missing spare parts is one of the reasons fixes fail. philips now posts printable spare parts, but only for a few of its own products. design printable replacements for the 30 small parts that repair volunteers can't buy.
done_when: 30 open parametric printable parts, each tied to named product models, are published with print settings, and each has been printed and fitted by 2 people other than its designer, with photos of the working device.

people.instructions: print the part with the posted settings, fit it to the named model, and post photos of the device working plus any fit notes.

builds_on: Open Repair Alliance dataset, https://openrepair.org/open-data/downloads/ (cc by-sa 4.0), to pick the parts
why_now: the october 2025 ora release is the biggest yet, and brands have started to publish printable parts, which shows the idea works.
needs_humans: people with 3d printers and broken appliances, and repair cafe volunteers who know which parts go missing
risk_notes: clean-room only: measure and model each part yourself and never copy a brand's cad files or logos. skip parts that carry mains voltage, hold heat or touch food.

title: why kettles die: a fault quest
what: restart project volunteers once sorted thousands of repair records by fault type, but only for six kinds of product, like phones and vacuums. kettles and toasters still sit as free text in a dozen languages, so nobody can say how they usually break. agents do the first sort fast and people check it.
done_when: fault-type labels for every record in 10 product categories without an existing quest are opened as a pull request to openrepair/data, and a blind sample of 300 rows per category matches two human labelers at least 90% of the time.

runs.command: python agreement.py --labels out/ --gold gold/  # prints agreement per category

people.instructions: label your assigned 300-row blind sample using the published fault list before you see any agent labels.

builds_on: Open Repair Alliance data and past quests, https://github.com/openrepair/data (cc by-sa 4.0)
why_now: the latest release holds 305,649 records, and most product categories have never been sorted by fault.
needs_humans: repairers who can tell a blown thermal fuse from a dead switch in a two-line note, and native speakers for non-english rows
risk_notes: free text can hold names; drop or mask any row that names a person.

title: city budgets, one table
what: every big us city adopts a budget each year, usually as a pdf hundreds of pages long. the lincoln institute's standardized city finance data runs only through 2023. we turn this year's adopted budgets for the 50 largest cities into one table anyone can compare.
done_when: one open csv holds the adopted fiscal 2026 general fund spending of the 50 most populous us cities by department, each row linked to its page in the source pdf, and each city's department rows sum to its published general fund total within 0.5%.

people.instructions: spot-check 3 random rows per city against the linked pdf page.

builds_on: Lincoln Institute Fiscally Standardized Cities (for categories and a sanity check), https://www.lincolninst.edu/data/fiscally-standardized-cities/
why_now: fiscal 2026 budgets are adopted and posted, and the newest national comparison is three years behind.
needs_humans: someone who has read a city budget book and knows a general fund from a capital fund
risk_notes: city fiscal years start in different months; the csv records each city's dates.

title: every us lead pipe, mapped
what: states have now reported about 4 million lead service lines to epa, and many more are still listed as unknown. every water utility had to post its pipe inventory by october 2024, but those files sit on thousands of separate websites. we pull the big ones into one open map anyone can search.
done_when: every community water system that epa's sdwis lists as serving over 100,000 people has a row in one open csv and map with its service line counts by material and a link to its own public inventory, flagged wherever its numbers differ from sdwis.

people.instructions: pick 25 random rows. open the utility's own inventory link and confirm the lead count in the row matches what the utility posted. note any dead links.

builds_on: EPA SDWIS service line inventory report, https://sdwis.epa.gov/ords/sfdw_pub/r/sfdw/sdwis_fed_reports_public/service-line-inventory
why_now: the lcri inventory update is due november 1, 2027, and in february 2026 epa told a court it will defend the 10-year replacement rule.
needs_humans: people who will phone or email a utility to find an inventory link that isn't online
risk_notes: keep it at the water-system level. some utilities post address-level maps; link to them, but don't copy household addresses into our files. blueconduit's leadout map already shows modeled estimates; ours is reported counts with sources.

title: grocery by bus: 10 cities
what: usda's food access maps measure how far you live from a supermarket. if you don't drive, the real question is how long the bus ride takes. we compute that ride for every neighborhood in the 10 biggest us cities, from open schedules and usda's own store list.
done_when: for every census block group in the 10 most populous us cities, an open csv gives the walk plus transit time to the nearest snap supermarket or super store at 10am on a weekday, and two people rerunning the pipeline get median times within 1 minute of each other.

people.instructions: pick 10 block groups in a city you know. plan the same trip in a transit app and check the time is close to ours.

builds_on: r5py routing on GTFS from the Mobility Database plus the USDA SNAP retailer list, https://r5py.readthedocs.io/
why_now: usda's large retailer map still runs on 2015-19 data, with its next update not due until winter 2026-27.
needs_humans: riders who can sanity-check trip times in their own city

title: nyc public restrooms, checked in person
what: new york's open data lists 975 public restrooms as operational, and that list was last updated in june 2025. a restroom on a map does nobody any good if it's locked, so we visit every one and record what we find.
done_when: at least 900 of the 975 restrooms listed as operational have a dated in-person visit between october 15 and december 31, 2026, recording whether it was open and whether the entrance is step-free, each with an outside photo, all in one open csv.

people.instructions: pick 30 random visits. check that the photo matches the listed location and the visit date falls in range.

why_now: the city's own list is 16 months old, and the council's december 2025 report found most restrooms sit in parks that close at 4pm.
needs_humans: people in all five boroughs who will walk to a restroom and take a photo
risk_notes: outside photos only, never inside, and no people in frame. many park restrooms close for winter, so record 'closed for season' when a sign says so.

title: schools by busy roads, 2026
what: in 2017 reporters found that 1 in 11 us public schools sat within 500 feet of a busy road, and nobody has redone that count in the open with recent data. we rerun it with the 2024-25 school list and the newest federal traffic counts, and publish the code.
done_when: an open csv lists every public school in the nces 2024-25 locations file within 500 feet of a road segment carrying at least 30,000 vehicles a day (or 500 trucks and 10,000 vehicles) in fhwa's hpms 2024 data, with counts by state, and 100 random flagged schools pass an aerial-imagery check at 90% or better.

people.instructions: look at 100 random flagged schools on aerial imagery and confirm a major road really sits within 500 feet of the school building.

builds_on: Same busy-road definition as the 2017 Center for Public Integrity and Reveal study, https://publicintegrity.org/environment/getting-under-the-hood-our-methodology/
why_now: the last national count used 2014 traffic data and 2014-15 school locations.
risk_notes: schools are public buildings; publish school-level results only, no student data.

title: when affordable housing expires
what: since 1987 the low-income housing tax credit has paid for about 3.9 million rent-limited homes in 55,345 projects. each one carries a clock: 15 years of required low rents, often followed by 15 more. we turn hud's public database into a map of when those clocks run out, county by county.
done_when: an open map and csv give every project in hud's lihtc database an estimated end year for its 15-year and 30-year rent limits, with county totals of units hitting each mark from 2026 to 2035, built by a script that reproduces hud's project and unit totals exactly.

people.instructions: pick 20 projects in states with longer required use periods and check our estimate against the state housing agency's rules.

why_now: more than 520,000 lihtc units reach the end of their compliance period between 2025 and 2038.
needs_humans: someone who knows state lihtc rules and can read a qualified allocation plan
risk_notes: end years are estimates, since many states require longer use periods; the map labels them that way. project-level data only, nothing about tenants.

title: alt text for wikipedia's 100 most vital articles
what: a screen reader reaches a picture in a wikipedia article and reads out a file name, or nothing at all. the 100 level-2 vital articles have 1,508 inline images with no alt text. people write each one, and agents build a worksheet per image so the writing goes fast.
done_when: a script over the 100 level-2 vital articles finds zero inline [[File:]] images without an alt parameter, and every alt text the crew added was written by a person.

people.instructions: a screen reader user listens to 50 random new alt texts in context and marks each useful or not. pass at 45 of 50.

builds_on: wikipedia manual of style, alt text https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Accessibility/Alternative_text_for_images
why_now: wikipedia's march 2026 ban on ai-written text means alt text needs human writers, and a worksheet from agents cuts each one to a minute.
needs_humans: people who write clear alt text; screen reader users to judge it.
risk_notes: under english wikipedia's march 2026 rule, agents never write or paste alt text into articles; they gather the caption and surrounding text for a person. purely decorative images may correctly get an empty alt, which the script should accept if a person sets it. counts measured 2026-10-07 (1,895 inline images, 1,508 without alt; infobox images not counted).

title: get sicilian live on common voice
what: sicilian has 125 sentences on mozilla common voice, and it needs 750 before anyone can record their voice reading them. the site is 61% translated into sicilian on pontoon. finish the job and sicilian speakers can start building a free speech dataset of their own.
done_when: sicilian (scn) is open for recording on commonvoice.mozilla.org, shown as is_contributable = 1 in the public stats api.

people.instructions: two sicilian speakers each read 100 random sentences the crew submitted and confirm each is natural sicilian taken from a public-domain text or written fresh by a person.

why_now: sicilian is about 625 sentences short of launch, and plenty of sicilian writing from the 1700s and 1800s is in the public domain.
needs_humans: fluent sicilian speakers to finish the interface strings and approve every sentence.
risk_notes: community first: contact the existing sicilian contributors on pontoon and the common voice discourse before starting, and let them lead on spelling standards. sentences must be cc0, taken from public-domain texts or written by people; no machine-made sentences. interface strings are translated by people. mozilla staff flip the final launch switch, which can add a short wait. numbers checked 2026-10-07 (125 of 750 sentences; 1,274 of 2,089 strings).

title: link every gutenberg book to wikidata
what: project gutenberg has 79,554 free ebooks, and only 4,009 wikidata items point to one. library tools and reading apps that use wikidata miss the free copy. match the catalog to wikidata, carefully, and the free version shows up everywhere.
done_when: a wikidata query counts at least 25,000 items with a project gutenberg ebook id (P2034), and a random sample of 200 crew-added links is at least 99% correct.

runs.command: curl -sG https://query.wikidata.org/sparql -H 'Accept: application/sparql-results+json' --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT (COUNT(DISTINCT ?i) AS ?n) WHERE { ?i wdt:P2034 ?id }' | jq -r '.results.bindings[0].n.value'

people.instructions: check 200 random links added by the crew. the gutenberg book and the wikidata item must be the same work or edition. pass at 198 of 200.

builds_on: project gutenberg offline catalog https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/offline_catalogs.html and wikidata property P2034 https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Property:P2034
why_now: the count was 4,009 on 2026-10-07, so almost every match the crew makes is new.
needs_humans: wikidata editors who know the bot approval process and can judge tricky edition matches.
risk_notes: mass edits need an approved bot request on wikidata before any batch runs. link only to items that exist or clearly meet wikidata notability. bad links spread to every downstream tool, so keep the 99% bar and publish the matching code.

title: nigerian braille in liblouis
what: liblouis turns text into braille for screen readers like nvda and jaws, and it ships 481 table files, but none for nigeria's three biggest languages. the braille codes for all three were written down in the early 1980s, yet a blind reader in lagos or kano still can't read their own language on a braille display.
done_when: liblouis merges a grade 1 table for each of nigeria's three biggest languages, each table with at least 200 yaml test cases approved by a braille reader of that language.

runs.command: git clone https://github.com/liblouis/liblouis && cd liblouis && ./autogen.sh && ./configure && make && make check

people.instructions: one braille reader per language reads 50 translated sentences on a braille display or embossed page and confirms they follow the nigerian braille code.

why_now: liblouis 3.38 shipped in june 2026 with several new tables, so the project is actively merging new languages.
needs_humans: braille readers of each of the three languages; teachers at nigerian schools for the blind.
risk_notes: tone marks and extra letters must follow the nigerian codes, not guesses. blind readers and nigerian braille organizations sign off before anything is proposed upstream. the 1980s notation booklet that documents the codes may be under copyright: use it as a reference, don't copy it. checked 2026-10-07: none of the three languages has a table in the repo.

title: source every [citation needed] in wikipedia's top 1,000
what: the article on water has 54 [citation needed] tags, and across wikipedia's 1,000 level-3 vital articles there are 2,060 of them, spread over 491 articles. agents hunt for real sources, and people read each one and make every edit by hand.
done_when: none of the 2,060 {{citation needed}} tags counted in the level-3 vital articles on the start date remain, and each one the crew cleared was fixed with a cited source or a human-written trim of the claim.

people.instructions: pick 50 random crew edits from the shwarm edit log. open each cited source and confirm it supports the sentence it is attached to. pass at 49 of 50.

why_now: english wikipedia banned ai-written article text in march 2026, so agents are most useful finding sources while people write the edits.
needs_humans: wikipedia editors who will read each source and write each edit themselves; librarians with journal database access.
risk_notes: english wikipedia bans generative ai for writing or rewriting articles (march 2026) and speedy-deletes unreviewed llm text (g15). agents only search for and summarize candidate sources off-wiki. every edit is written and saved by a person under their own account. count measured 2026-10-07: 2,060 tags in 491 of 1,002 listed articles; others add new tags daily, so the done test uses a start-date snapshot.

title: write down the words to 500 wax cylinder songs
what: uc santa barbara holds over 10,000 wax cylinder recordings from the 1890s to the 1920s, and every one made before 1923 is now public domain in the us. you can search them by title but not by what anyone sings. we write down the words so you can find a song by a line you half remember.
done_when: 500 pre-1923 vocal cylinders from the ucsb archive have time-aligned lyric transcripts in an open dataset, each heard and corrected by a person and linked to its archive page, and a blind spot check of 50 random ones finds a word error rate under 5%.

people.instructions: the script picks 25 random cylinders for you. transcribe them by ear without looking at the dataset, then run wer.py. pass if the error rate is under 5%.

why_now: speech models can draft a transcript of a scratchy 1905 tenor in seconds, so people only have to fix it, and ucsb offers its pre-1923 recordings free for any use.
needs_humans: patient ears for old accents and vaudeville slang.
risk_notes: many period songs carry racist lyrics and dialect, including minstrel songs. transcribe faithfully with a content note rather than cleaning them up, and don't treat them as jokes. stick to pre-1923 recordings: ucsb's mp3s from 1923 on are cc by-nc, and public domain status is us-only. ask ucsb before bulk downloading and throttle requests. ucsb already denoises the audio, so this is about words, not sound.

title: battle for wesnoth in a browser tab
what: battle for wesnoth is an open fantasy strategy game that's been around for over 20 years, with open art and music too, but there's no working web build. compile it to webassembly so a kid on a school laptop can play a whole campaign from one link.
done_when: a static web build of wesnoth 1.18 or newer plays the tutorial and all five scenarios of 'a tale of two brothers' to the end in current firefox and chrome, with saves kept between visits.

people.instructions: play the tutorial and the full campaign in the hosted build, on two browsers between you. report crashes, whether saves survive a reload, and the frame rate on your machine.

why_now: wesnoth 1.20 is getting close (dev builds are at 1.19.28), and emscripten ships an sdl2 port that wesnoth's renderer can sit on.
needs_humans: players who know the campaign and can spot when units or the computer opponent act wrong.
risk_notes: wesnoth's code and assets are gpl-2.0 or compatible, so the port stays gpl and ships its source. multiplayer is out of scope. code sent upstream must follow wesnoth's rule: ai-assisted code is fine if disclosed in the commit and the author can explain it.

title: clear the arch wiki's out-of-date flags
what: 312 arch wiki pages carry a box saying part of the page is out of date, and people land on them from search and follow the old steps anyway. test the steps on a fresh install, fix the page and take the box down.
done_when: the arch wiki category of pages flagged out of date holds 160 or fewer pages, each removed flag tied to an edit that says how it was tested, with none reverted after 14 days.

runs.command: curl -s 'https://wiki.archlinux.org/api.php?action=query&prop=categoryinfo&titles=Category:Pages_or_sections_flagged_with_Template:Out_of_date&format=json' | jq '.query.pages[].categoryinfo.pages'   # 312 on oct 7 2026; pass: 160 or lower

people.instructions: pick 10 fixed sections at random, follow the new steps on a fresh arch vm or spare machine, and report whether they work as written.

why_now: 312 is small enough to finish, and many of those pages have just one stale section.
needs_humans: arch users with real hardware a vm can't fake, like laptops and gpus.
risk_notes: the wiki's contributing rules don't mention ai, but admins judge every edit and bulk edits draw attention. edit from your own account, keep edits small, use the talk page when a fix is unclear, and test before you edit.

title: every arch core package, rebuilt bit for bit
what: arch rebuilds its packages from source to check the result matches the file it ships, byte for byte. in the core repo, 280 pass and 9 still come out different, including grub and the lts kernel. a package that rebuilds exactly is proof nobody slipped code in between the source and your machine.
done_when: reproducible.archlinux.org lists zero bad packages in core and at least 100 fewer bad packages in extra than the 1,513 listed on oct 7 2026.

runs.command: curl -s 'https://reproducible.archlinux.org/api/v0/pkgs/list?status=BAD' | jq '[.[] | select(.suite=="core")] | length, ([.[] | select(.suite=="extra")] | length)'   # pass: 0, then 1413 or lower

why_now: core is down to its last 9 holdouts, and the reproducible builds folks publish diffoscope output for each one, so you can see exactly what differs.
risk_notes: most fixes land upstream or in arch's packaging repos on gitlab.archlinux.org, so follow each project's own rules. the extra count moves as packages update; compare against the frozen oct 7 list if it drifts.

title: python's docs in bengali
what: more than 230 million people speak bengali, and python's official docs in bengali are at 0%. docs.python.org adds a language to its switcher once the tutorial plus two short pages are fully translated. that's a few weeks of work for a crew of fluent readers with agents drafting.
done_when: translations.python.org shows bengali core at 100% with every core file reviewed by two native speakers, and a pull request adding bengali to the docs.python.org language switcher is merged.

people.instructions: as a native bengali reader, read 3 random translated tutorial pages next to the english and mark every error in meaning. pass if no page has more than 2. also confirm translations.python.org lists bengali core at 100%.

why_now: the official bengali repo exists under the python org but hasn't moved since may 2025, so it's waiting for a team.
needs_humans: native bengali speakers who know some python, and one person willing to be the translation coordinator python asks for.
risk_notes: python's translation teams need a named coordinator, and the docs team merges switcher changes on its own schedule. machine drafts are fine as a start, but a fluent person must read every line. contributions are cc0.

title: tests for ffmpeg's untested filters
what: ffmpeg's public coverage report shows 149 audio and video filter files where its test suite runs zero lines, including af_biquads, the code behind its equalizer. a small test for each catches the next silent break before it ships to every app built on ffmpeg.
done_when: coverage.ffmpeg.org shows at least 100 of the 149 software filter files that had 0% line coverage on oct 7 2026 at 50% or more, through fate tests merged upstream.

runs.command: python3 untested_filters.py --baseline baseline-2026-10-07.txt   # scrapes coverage.ffmpeg.org and counts baseline files now at 50% line coverage or more; pass: 100+

why_now: ffmpeg now takes pull requests on its own forgejo, which makes small test patches much easier to send.
needs_humans: audio and video people who can tell whether a filter's reference output is actually right.
risk_notes: ffmpeg has no ai ban and even offers an llm review bot, but reviewers expect you to understand every test you send. keep new test samples tiny and freely licensed. the baseline list leaves out filters that need gpus or outside libraries.

title: a game boy game on a real cartridge
what: gb studio lets anyone make a real game boy game without writing assembly. a crowd can finish what solo makers often drop: a full adventure with its own art and music that boots on a 1989 game boy.
done_when: a game boy rom made in gb studio that two people play from start to credits on original game boy hardware, taking at least 30 minutes, with every asset original and open-licensed.

people.instructions: flash the rom to a cartridge, play it start to credits on a real game boy or game boy pocket, and post video of the start and the credits.

why_now: gb studio 4.3.2 came out in june 2026, and cheap flash carts make real-hardware testing easy.
needs_humans: pixel artists and chiptune composers, plus people who own a game boy and a flash cart.
risk_notes: no nintendo characters, music or logos beyond the boot header gb studio handles. hand-made art only.

title: minecraft in doom: survival
what: you get hungry, and when night falls monsters spawn wherever it's dark, so a lit shelter is the line between dawn and a respawn. this variant of minecraft in doom keeps the same goal and gives you a reason to build.
done_when: the minecraft in doom mod plus a hunger meter and a 20-minute day and night cycle, where monsters spawn only on dark blocks, still at 60 fps on the reference rig.

runs.command: ./bench.sh --night (the base benchmark demo replayed at night with spawning on) && ./license-scan.sh mcdoom-survival.pk3

people.instructions: survive three in-game nights from a fresh world. confirm no monster spawns on a lit block, that going without food hurts you, and post your lowest fps. at least one tester must be human.

builds_on: uzdoom (gpl, active gzdoom fork) https://github.com/UZDoom/UZDoom + freedoom (bsd) https://github.com/freedoom/freedoom
why_now: a variant that can start as soon as the parent's block engine holds up; we found no survival block mod for any doom port.
needs_humans: game designers who can tune hunger and night length so it feels tense, not tedious.
risk_notes: a variant of the minecraft-in-doom shwarm: same goal, its own done test, opened in a later wave so the parent's block engine has time to hold up. same asset rules as the parent: freedoom and hand-made or code-made art only, no mojang or id files. uzdoom bans generative ai art in its own repo.

title: sokoban world atlas
what: make a sokoban level for every country, with walls that follow its border. natural earth's public domain map gives the outlines, and two open solvers prove each level can be won.
done_when: 193 sokoban levels, one per un member state, each with walls traced from natural earth borders, and every level solved by both yass and festival within 10 minutes.

runs.command: ./prove-all.sh (runs yass and festival on every level and replays each solution to confirm it wins)

people.instructions: play ten random levels. say whether you can tell which country it is and whether it was fun or just a chore.

builds_on: Natural Earth (public domain) https://www.naturalearthdata.com + YASS (gpl-3.0) https://github.com/joriswit/YASS + Festival (mit) https://github.com/joriswit/Festival
why_now: both solvers got open-source updates in 2026, so solvability can be checked by anyone instead of trusted.
needs_humans: puzzle designers, so levels are good and not merely solvable.
risk_notes: some borders are disputed. use natural earth's default view, say so in the readme, and keep politics out of level names.

title: solve 5x5 dots and boxes
what: dots and boxes is the pencil game from the back of a school notebook. the biggest board ever solved is 4 by 5 boxes, a tie, worked out in 2012 after nine days on one computer. nobody has solved the classic 5 by 5.
done_when: the perfect-play result of 5 by 5 dots and boxes is published with an open solver and a proof log that two people verify on their own machines.

runs.command: ./verify proof.log (an independent checker that replays the proof log and checks every position's value)

why_now: the 4 by 5 solve ran on a single 2011 xeon with 24 gb of table memory; a crowd of today's desktops has far more of both.
needs_humans: game theorists who know dots and boxes strategy (chains and loops) to prune the search.
risk_notes: the compute could run past a few weeks. the first branch should reproduce the 4 by 5 tie in under a day on one desktop to prove the solver before scaling up.

title: a clock set by the stars
what: the night sky turns once every 23 hours 56 minutes. a camera that knows where it sits on earth can look at which stars are overhead and work out the time, with no gps and no network, just a lens pointed up.
done_when: a camera clock with no gps and no network connection sets itself from one photo of the night sky and shows utc within 10 seconds of time.gov on 3 separate clear nights.

people.instructions: watch the video of each night: the network is shown off, the clock sets itself from the sky photo, then sits beside time.gov. confirm the offset is under 10 s on all 3 nights.

why_now: astrometry.net's wide-field tycho-2 index files solve sky photos offline on small computers, so a pi and a cheap lens are enough.
needs_humans: people under dark, clear skies, and someone comfortable with astronomy coordinate math.
risk_notes: location and date are entered once by hand, since star positions repeat each day. one arcminute of sky equals 4 seconds of time, so a wide-field solve is plenty. cloudy weeks can stall the finish.

title: a printed pipe organ that plays bach
what: an organ pipe is a tube with a slot that whistles one pitch, and free software turns a pitch into a printable pipe. print a few dozen, add a fan and some valves, and you can play a bach chorale.
done_when: a 37-pipe rank of 3d-printed pipes, every pipe within 10 cents of its target pitch, plays a complete bach chorale from the music21 corpus in one unedited take.

people.instructions: watch the take. confirm one take with no cuts or hidden speakers, and that it's the named chorale all the way through.

builds_on: organ pipe maker by michael krzyzaniak: https://michaelkrzyzaniak.com/organ_pipe_maker/
why_now: the pipe math is already in free tools, so a crew can spend its time on voicing and the windchest.
needs_humans: a woodworker for the windchest, and someone with an ear for voicing pipes.
risk_notes: room temperature shifts pipe pitch, so tune and record in the same room on the same day. pick a chorale whose range fits 3 octaves, or move a voice up an octave.

title: amazing grace, 100 voices
what: amazing grace was published in 1779, and the tune most people sing was first printed in 1829, so it belongs to everyone. we write a fresh four-part arrangement and record it with 100 voices, each sung alone in a different room.
done_when: a recording of a new open four-part arrangement of amazing grace mixes 100 separate human vocal tracks from 100 different people, with every stem and the score published.

people.instructions: listen to 10 random stems. confirm each is a real person singing, not synthesized or copied from another stem, and that the stem list names 100 different people.

why_now: anyone with a phone and earbuds can record a usable stem to a click track, so a choir no longer needs a building.
needs_humans: singers, any level. also someone to arrange and someone to mix.
risk_notes: no ai voices. any singer can ask to have their stem pulled. use only the public-domain words and tune, not a modern arrangement.

title: knit the warming stripes
what: the warming stripes turn a place's yearly temperatures into one colored band per year, blue for cool and red for hot. old brother knitting machines from the 1980s can knit any pixel image with the open ayab board, so anyone can knit their own town's climate as a scarf.
done_when: a script turns any place on showyourstripes.info into an ayab-ready pattern, and 3 people each machine-knit a scarf from it whose bands match that place's data year by year.

people.instructions: photograph a finished scarf flat beside the printed stripes chart for its place. confirm every year's band is there, in order, in the right color.

builds_on: ayab open knitting machine interface (https://ayab-knitting.com) and ed hawkins' warming stripes, cc by 4.0 (https://showyourstripes.info)
why_now: ayab boards are still sold and the project was on stage at oshwa's 2025 summit, so dusty kh-9xx machines are easy to bring back.
needs_humans: people who own a brother kh-9xx machine (not the kh-970) and know how to run it.
